Senses.Explanation: In Chan records, the headword is the respectful title used to address or identify a senior monastic master. Huike addresses Bodhidharma; Huang Tingjian addresses the senior monastic before him; Guishan Lingyou and Zhaozhou Congshen address their teachers; Linji Yixuan and Huangbo Xiyun speak of the old masters under heaven. Compiler narration also attaches the title to Wuzu Fayan, Budai Qici, Master An of Songshan, and Wuzu Jie. Direct address, honorific naming, and collective description retain the same senior-master referent; a narrator’s title is not an utterance by its bearer.
Senses.Note: Ten exact witnesses from ten distinct works cover address, title, collective description, and named designation. The nested ‘sons of masters’ compound was excluded under the substring gate and supplies no bare-headword plural-vocative sense.

Senses.Explanation: mixing (和) mud (泥) and blending (合) water (水): “mixing mud and blending water.” Chan records make the ordinary mixing image an appraisal of sayings, explanations, and speakers. In a recasting of three phrases, "understanding from the first phrase" is called "mixing mud and blending water," followed by "binding oneself without a rope" and "landing with all four edges on the ground" (第一句薦得，和泥合水；第二句薦得，無繩自縛；第三句薦得，四稜著地). Another record groups it with "speaking a dream without a dream" and "not knowing good from bad" (無夢說夢，和泥合水，撒屎撒尿，不識好惡). Yet the phrase also stands as a direct answer to "what is the true source of the great road?" (如何是大道真源), and one discourse pairs "where wind cannot enter" with "mixing mud and blending water" in both directions. Another contrasts failing to mark the moment, when black and white remain undistinguished, with marking it too late, called "mixing mud and blending water." These are different recorded placements of one image. The texts do not supply the uniform gloss “descending to the student's level,” so neither does this entry.

Senses.Explanation: A ‘Continuation of the Lamp Record’ is a later lineage history that extends earlier lamp records with additional masters, cases, and succession claims. The title names the Song compilation submitted by Fogu Weibai, while Guxue Zhe describes compiling Yuan- and Ming-period masters into a later continuation. Shuijian Huihai and Langting Jingting cite or dispute what such a record says about Xuedou Chongxian’s lineage. In these records the title is therefore not only bibliographic: its contents are evidence contested in public lineage adjudication.

Senses.Note: One person sense. Zhigong (誌公), Master Zhigong (誌公和尚), name the same figure in this corpus. Titles of works attributed to him are named works, not a second sense of the bare personal name.

Senses.Explanation: Master Zhigong is the pre-Zen figure whom Chan records quote, identify with a direct answer, and place in exchanges at Emperor Wu's court. His name occurs 494 times in 133 allowlisted texts. Asked "what is buddha?" Wanan Daoyan answers, "Master Zhigong" (誌公和尚); when challenged, he says, "Zhigong is not an idle monk" (誌公不是閑和尚). In the Fu Dashi case, Fu mounts the seat, strikes the desk once, and descends; Zhigong asks Emperor Wu whether he understands, then says, "the great man has finished lecturing the scripture" (大士講經竟). Later masters repeatedly quote and criticize that verdict. His sayings are also treated as named textual material: the Twelve-Hour Song, Fourteen Sections, and Great-Vehicle Praises. Zen therefore deploys Zhigong as a named answer to "what is buddha?," court interlocutor and adjudicator of Fu Dashi's action, and quoted author.
